phase-checkpointed, resumable, dry-run, per-server lock via `Job.serverId`, automatic rollback before
`COMMIT`, source VM kept STOPPED with `onboot=0` + tag `nxeon-moved` for 7 days, explicit cleanup).
Transfer = two-pass **ZFS send/receive** over zstd (consistent guest-agent snapshot while running, then
a stopped-VM incremental — dark window ≈ 3–5 min); `qm remote-migrate` rejected (still EXPERIMENTAL on
PVE 9.2, needs `VM.Migrate` the platform token lacks, `--online` unsafe across the fleet's mixed
`cpu: host` CPU models, no incremental offline) and vzdump→restore kept only as the manual fallback.
Dedicated IPs travel: OVH `GET /ip/{ip}/move` is the authoritative same-campus guard (verified live: a
Singapore IP lists the three SGP boxes and not `ns565008` in Beauharnois), then `POST /ip/{ip}/move` +
task poll + a new Virtual MAC on the target server — the LAST step before start, with rollback moving
it back. The guest boots on the target with a **move-safe vendor snippet** (`ssh_deletekeys: false`,
agent + root SSH only) because Proxmox's NoCloud instance-id changes with the network config and would
otherwise re-run the original provisioning `runcmd` and regenerate SSH host keys. Node-agent v2 gained
`/v1/zfs/{dataset,snapshot,recv,send}` (same allowlists as `lib/vm-move/plan.ts`; refuses any dataset
whose vmid has a VM config on that node; `requestTimeout: 0` for the multi-GB upload); until every
node runs v2, `VM_MOVE_TRANSPORT=ssh` is the documented transition fallback. Target vmid is
`pickMoveTargetVmid()`: strictly above every id seen on any node, in `Server`/`ServerArchive`/`VmMove`
and the target's backup archives (never a recycled id; 9000–9999 skipped). Admin interface for the ops
UI: `lib/vm-move/actions.ts` (`requestVmMove`, `previewVmMove`, `getVmMove`, `listVmMoves`,
`listMoveCandidates`, `requestVmMoveRollback`, `requestVmMoveCleanup`), all `requireArea("fleet")`
+ audited. Pure planning logic (vmid choice, capacity verdicts from REAL available RAM, candidate
classes A/B/C + ranking, phase machine, rollback inventory, target config derivation, OVH destination
guard) is covered by `test/vm-move-plan.test.ts`.

**Found while vetting (not fixed):** VMs 106 `nexis-app` and 110 `kodely-app` are RUNNING on Proxmox
while their `Server` rows say STOPPED; 106's `ipconfig0` still carries `51.79.226.215`, a customer's
dedicated IP that now lives on node-3; `projectzomboid-kc0kcr`, `upnormal` and `sausaugepro` each exist
on two nodes (node-2 leftovers, `sausaugepro` running on both); node-5's 20 GB root disk is 96 % full
(its `backup` dir storage sits on it); `bujangsmp`'s term ended 2026-09-30 with auto-renew on.

**Not done:** the rehearsal move (the primary had 1.3 GB root-disk free and 6 GB RAM during this work;
cloning a VM onto it was the wrong call today — protocol in the plan doc §6); deploying agent v2 to the
nodes; `prisma db push`; any host-level change (every quick win is given as an exact command for the owner).

**Files:** `prisma/schema.prisma`, `lib/vm-move/*`, `worker/vm-move.ts`, `worker/index.ts` (handler
registration), `lib/node-agent.ts` (zfs client calls), `node-agent/index.js` (v2 endpoints),
`test/vm-move-plan.test.ts`, `docs/VM-MOVE.md`, `docs/PRIMARY-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md`.

### 2026-10-01 — VM move engine: deep analysis + hardening (branch `feature/vm-move-hardening`, NOT promoted)

Adversarial review of the same-day VM_MOVE engine before it ever touches a customer
(`docs/VM-MOVE-DEEP-ANALYSIS.md`: completeness matrix, FMEA, rehearsal plan, go/no-go).
  re-ran it, and each retry minted a management key the guest never received.
- **Not the cause:** an SSH exec timeout on the pull. Provisioning never runs the pull over SSH.

**Shipped:**
- node-side IP inventory in IPAM, plus re-checking a retry's address;
- stored-credential login with a guest-agent repair, and SMBIOS-UUID identity checks before anything
  runs;
- management-key reuse on retries;
- retried, idempotent, observable in-guest game setup, launched via `systemd-run`;
- guest-evidence startup verdicts with the game's own last lines in `Job.error`;
- `ProvisionStopError` (no retry for deterministic failures);
- PZ `ADMIN_USERNAME` default `admin`, and blank identity values never override the catalog;
- unit restart backoff;
- node-agent v4 `GET /v1/net/neigh`;
- report-only `fleet-ip-audit` sweep, plus scripts `fleet-ip-audit.ts` and

19703:## Bedrock never opens its game port: NetherNet default, TRANSPORT=raknet, pinned "Latest" (2026-10-06)
19726:## Invoices: real logo + multi-line line items (2026-10-06)
**Incident.** Every fresh Minecraft Bedrock deploy failed provisioning with `game port 19132/udp never opened ... ECONNREFUSED`, on every node and plan. The container started, logged `Server started.` and docker reported healthy, but no game UDP socket existed (`/proc/net/udp` empty in the container; the `IPv4 supported, port: 19132` line was missing).

**Root cause.** Since BDS 1.26.50 Mojang's default `transport` in server.properties is `nethernet` (WebRTC: one dual-stack TCP signalling socket on `server-port`, UDP negotiated per client), not `raknet` (UDP 19132/19133). A server.properties generated by BDS >= 1.26.50 therefore listens on 19132/**TCP** and binds no game UDP port. We publish `19132/udp` only, and `VERSION=LATEST` resolved to 1.26.52.3, so every fresh data dir got the NetherNet default. Servers whose server.properties was written by an older BDS keep `transport=raknet` in the file (verified: a 1.26.45.1-created file keeps it through an in-place upgrade to 52.3), which is why the two live customers (upnormal, suplosmp) were unaffected. Mojang has announced NetherNet becomes the only transport from BDS 1.26.60 (RakNet removed).

**Version matrix** (fresh data dir, throwaway VM; "RakNet ping" = unconnected ping to the published UDP port answered with a pong):

| BDS | default transport | with `TRANSPORT=raknet` |
|---|---|---|
| 1.26.45.1 | raknet: UDP 19132/19133 open, ping OK | same, ping OK |
| 1.26.50.5 | nethernet: TCP 19132 only, no UDP, ping fails | UDP open, ping OK (logs a TRANSPORT TYPE ERROR notice) |
| 1.26.51.1 | nethernet, same | UDP open, ping OK (notice) |
| 1.26.52.3 | nethernet, same | UDP open, ping OK (notice) |

Mojang download URLs that exist (2026-10-06): 1.26.40.8, 42.1, 43.1, 44.3, 45.1, 50.5, 51.1, 52.3. Not verified with a real game client (only the server side); the 50+ builds print a notice saying NetherNet is the only supported transport but still serve RakNet.

**Fix.** `lib/bedrock-version.ts` is the single place: `BEDROCK_KNOWN_GOOD_VERSION` (1.26.52.3) and `BEDROCK_TRANSPORT` (raknet). `applyBedrockSetup` (called from `buildGameSetupScript`) resolves `VERSION=LATEST` to the pin, keeps explicit versions and PREVIEW, and adds `-e TRANSPORT=raknet` to every Bedrock container. The settings re-apply (`applyBedrock`) carries the same env. The stored value stays `LATEST` (existing rows valid); the wizard/settings label now reads "Recommended (Nxeon-tested build ...)". A Bedrock "port never opened" provision failure now appends the likely cause (`bedrockStartupHint`) to the admin-visible error. Seeds updated for fresh databases.

**Existing servers.** The container env bakes `VERSION=LATEST` and itzg re-resolves it on every container start, so every restart upgrades to the newest Mojang build; today that is harmless (their server.properties already says raknet) but a future 1.26.60 would break them on the next restart. `scripts/bedrock-protect.ts` (dry run by default; `--apply <hostname>` recreates the `bedrock` container with the pinned VERSION and TRANSPORT=raknet, brief restart, rollback on failure) closes that. Never run it without the owner's approval.

**How to bump the pin safely.** Change the one constant `BEDROCK_KNOWN_GOOD_VERSION`, after first running a throwaway Bedrock server on the new build with the exact flags (`-e TRANSPORT=raknet -p 19132:19132/udp -v ...:/data`) and confirming: the log has `IPv4 supported, port: 19132`, `/proc/net/udp` in the container lists 19132, a RakNet unconnected ping gets a 0x1c pong, and `npx tsx scripts/verify-game-provision.ts <hostname>` reports ports-guest PASS. Do not bump to 1.26.60+ until NetherNet (TCP signalling plus a UDP range) is implemented. Also keep `BEDROCK_RELEASE_VERSIONS` in lib/game-config.ts (the auto-update "newest curated" source) free of builds without RakNet.

## Invoices: real logo + multi-line line items (2026-10-06)

Both invoice renderers (`renderInvoiceHTML` in `lib/invoices.ts`, `renderInvoicePDF` in `lib/invoice-pdf.ts`) now draw the real Nxeon logo (`public/logo.png`, white wordmark made for dark backgrounds) on a navy header band (`INVOICE_HEADER_NAVY` = `#0a101f`, `--navy-900`) under the gradient bar; the invoice number and status stamp sit on the band. The old drawn "N" square is gone from the HTML.

- **HTML** uses an absolute URL, `appOrigin()/logo.png`, so a saved/emailed copy still shows it. `print-color-adjust: exact` keeps the band in print.
- **White-label rule:** the Nxeon logo is shown only when `brand_name` is the default "Nxeon" (`invoiceUsesNxeonLogo`). Any other brand name shows that name as white text on the band; the Nxeon logo is never presented as another brand.
- **PDF** embeds the PNG with `doc.image`. `loadInvoiceLogo()` reads it once and caches it, trying `process.cwd()/public/logo.png`, then `../public`, then relative to the module, then `/opt/nxeon/public/logo.png`. If no candidate is a readable PNG (or pdfkit rejects it), it draws the old gradient mark plus the brand name. It never throws, so invoice emails are unaffected.
- **Multi-line descriptions:** a line item `description` may contain `\n`. The first line is the headline; the rest are smaller muted sub-lines (HTML `.dsub`, PDF 9pt muted). Everything is escaped. `invoiceDescriptionLines()` drops blank lines and caps each item at 12 lines / 600 characters. A single-line description renders as before. PDF row height now includes the sub-lines, and a row that will not fit moves to a new page.
- Tests: `test/invoice-logo.test.ts`.

content.thinking:
Node-4's load ratio works out to around 5.1x on its vCPU-to-thread basis, well above node-primary's 3.25 and node-2's 1.9, so a default threshold of 4 would flag node-4 as already overloaded and block new provisions there if CPU-aware hard capping is enabled. I need to check whether that's actually the right call, since node-4 shares sgp1 with node-6 and two nodes that already have provisioning disabled.

I'm working out a scoring approach: compute capacity per node based on its shared-pool thread count times a ratio, project CPU usage as committed-plus-planned vCPU over that capacity, and only call a node "roomy" if both RAM and CPU projections stay under the critical threshold. Strict placement would refuse nodes that aren't roomy, while non-strict mode falls back to the existing least-bad logic, with an added hard rule excluding reserved nodes outright if a single VM's vCPU would exceed the shared pool's capacity on its own.

I'm also weighing how this interacts with regionAvailability's strict mode versus placeInRegion's non-strict mode — I don't want CPU pressure on node-4 to suddenly make sgp1 show as sold out to customers, so I'm considering making CPU a hard block only on nodes with reservations, while treating it as a soft scoring factor elsewhere.

So I'm defining a `scheduler_cpu_mode` setting with three levels: "off" keeps legacy RAM-only behavior but still hard-caps the shared pool on reservation nodes to protect other tenants and the host; "guard" (the default) adds that same hard CPU cap on reserved nodes to the legacy RAM scoring; and "score" extends this further by folding combined RAM/CPU headroom into scoring and roominess checks across all nodes.

The brief wants candidates scored on both RAM and CPU headroom with the behavior gated behind a setting for rollback safety, which makes me lean toward defaulting to "score" mode — but I'm wary of the visible fallout, like node-4's 5x ratio pushing it past the roomy threshold and potentially causing sgp1 to sell out under strict region availability. I'm weighing what default `cpu_overcommit_ratio` value would keep nodes like node-4 just under the warning threshold without being too conservative.

I think the safer path is to make CPU only count toward ranking/tie-breaking on non-reserved nodes, not toward the hard roomy/strict refusal logic, which stays limited to shared pools of reserved nodes like node-6. That way no existing node flips its region availability, but placement still leans toward CPU-lighter nodes — and rollback just means setting the mode to "off" (legacy) or "guard" (node-6 only). Still, I'm noting this could shift which node wins placement within sgp1, since node-4 and node-6 are both currently accepting and have different RAM headroom.

Checking the actual numbers: node-4 is already RAM-overcommitted while node-6 has real free RAM, so RAM alone already favors node-6. With a CPU guard on node-6's shared pool, I need to account for host overhead too, so I'm considering a separate overcommit ratio setting for that shared pool rather than reusing the general one.

I'll settle on a single overcommit ratio (default 4) applied everywhere instead of adding extra knobs, letting node-6 absorb up to 8 vCPU of guest load on top of its 2 host threads — fine for light VPS workloads but not CPU-heavy game servers, which I'll flag in the report.

For scoring, I'm weighting projected free RAM and CPU fractions (0.6/0.4) rather than sorting by raw free MB like the legacy approach, since fractional scoring changes which nodes get favored — this stays gated behind the setting. For thread topology, I still need to pull data either from the node agent's topology endpoint or the Proxmox node API.

I'll add cached fields on Node for thread count and topology JSON, refreshed by the periodic sweep, with the scheduler reading those cached values and falling back to a live Proxmox status call only if needed, since repeated live reads per scheduling decision would be too slow.

When topology or thread count is unavailable, I'll treat CPU scoring for that node as neutral rather than failing, while still requiring topology to exist for any node with CPU reservations since validation depends on it. I'm designing an additive CpuReservation model keyed to server and node, storing a canonical cpuset string plus core count.

Uniqueness is enforced per server, with overlap checks happening in code via transaction locking rather than database constraints. On the Node side I'm adding topology metadata and a derived, cached sharedCpuset field for debugging and agent views, while keeping the reservations table as the actual source of truth.

Going with a CpuReservation table approach plus Node.cpuTopology JSON and a timestamp, computing the shared/complement set rather than hard-storing it as the primary source. I also want drift-tracking fields on the reservation (lastVerifiedAt, lastDriftAt, lastDriftDetail) and need to check how existing NodeAlert/notifyAdmins mechanisms work so I can reuse them with deduplication for drift alerts, and I still need to handle what happens to a reservation when its server enters a DELETING state.

Once a reservation is removed, the node's shared pool should automatically widen back on the next sweep, so I need to decide which nodes get swept — only those with active reservations, or also those with lingering VM affinity settings that need clearing. The simplest approach is to sweep every node running agent v5 (or the primary agent) via a single GET call to the node's cpu/affinity endpoint, which returns all VMs' configured and live affinity in one request rather than hitting each VM individually.

I'm also wary of clearing affinity on nodes without reservations, since an admin may have manually pinned a VM, so I'd rather not touch those nodes except through the explicit provisioning apply-step. Instead, when the last reservation on a node is removed, that removal action itself should enqueue a node-wide apply job to widen all VMs — so the sweep only needs to target nodes with at least one active reservation or a cpuPoolManaged flag.

On the job type side, I'm checking whether I need a new enum value for this reservation-release sync job, and whether Job.serverId can be nullable; since this would go through the existing job/agent audited path, adding an enum value should be a safe, additive change.

Since tests run on the real production Proxmox host, I need to be careful that my agent test never triggers an actual `qm set` call on a live VM. I'm considering making the command binaries injectable via environment variables like NXEON_AGENT_QM_BIN and NXEON_AGENT_TASKSET_BIN, though I want to think through whether letting env vars override binaries creates a privilege-widening risk, especially since that env would be set by root in /etc/nxeon.

Since only index.js gets deployed to the agent, I can't split logic into a separate module — instead I should make the file dual-purpose by exporting functions and only starting the HTTP server when run directly via require.main === module. I also need to move the token-presence check into that same conditional block so requiring the file for tests doesn't kill the process.

For testing the real endpoint, I'll inject a system object (qmSet, readProc, etc.) so unit tests can swap in fakes rather than spawning actual qm/taskset commands. For HTTP-level tests against a genuinely spawned agent, I'll only send invalid inputs since validation rejects before touching the real system — a valid request would actually mutate a VM's CPU pinning. The GET topology endpoint reading /proc and qm list is read-only and safe to call live, though I'll keep it scoped to a nonexistent vmid to stay light.

Now I'm sketching the actual affinity endpoints: GET /v1/cpu/affinity reads each VM's config directly from /etc/pve/qemu-server/*.conf and cross-references live thread CPU masks via /proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/status, avoiding taskset entirely. The POST /v1/vm/affinity endpoint validates vmid and cpuset format against the online CPU set, then applies the affinity through qm set and, if live and running, propagates the change to each task thread in /proc.

For safety I should refuse templates, refuse VMs with no conf on this node, and verify the pid actually belongs to that vmid by checking /var/run/qemu-server/<vmid>.pid plus the cmdline's `-id` argument to avoid PID-reuse issues. I'm also unsure whether qm set --affinity on a running VM applies the change live in PVE 8+ versus requiring the manual taskset fallback — worth digging into the qemu-server hotplug source to confirm.

Since my endpoint applies taskset unconditionally whenever the VM is running, this behaves idempotently regardless of whether qm set applies it live. I still need to figure out how qm set handles pending changes versus the live config — I should parse /etc/pve's conf file directly, separating the main section from any [PENDING] block, and let pending affinity (including delete markers) override the main value. I'll check node-6's actual conf for VM 667 read-only to see where affinity currently lives.

content.thinking:
I'm thinking about how Proxmox applies CPU affinity to QEMU processes at startup, and whether that affinity actually propagates to related kernel threads like vhost-net, which live as separate kernel threads outside the normal process task list.

Setting affinity restricts VM processes but not host services like ZFS or pveproxy, which still run across all CPUs including reserved ones — this is a risk worth flagging. I'm also working out the topology validation rules: reservations must align to whole physical cores, never consume the last free core, avoid overlapping with existing reservations, only reference online CPUs, and ideally warn when vCPU count exceeds reserved threads, plus require the topology data be reasonably fresh.

For applying affinity, I'm thinking through the flow: the admin action reads live topology from the agent (or locally on the primary), validates it, and stores it on Node.cpuTopology. Since the web app runs on the primary itself, it can read /sys directly there, while execution of the actual `qm set` affinity change goes through the worker via a queued job rather than the web app doing it directly — I need a local equivalent of the agent's topology-reading functions for the primary node.

Rather than duplicating the agent's parsing logic in TS, I'm considering keeping all node I/O exclusively in the worker, with the web app only reading cached Node.cpuTopology from the DB and relying on periodic worker sweeps or a manual "refresh topology" job to keep it current — the worker re-validates against live topology right before applying anyway, so this cached-read approach is safe and keeps the web app agent-call-free. The core cpuset parsing and validation logic still needs to live in a shared TS lib so both sides can use it consistently.

For the worker's local primary-node operations, I'm planning a cpu-affinity module that wraps filesystem reads plus `qm`/`taskset` calls to expose topology, affinity, and setAffinity functions. To avoid re-implementing the same /proc parsing twice, I'm weighing having the worker directly require the node-agent's JS module at runtime via a resolved path, so primary-node handling shares the exact same code path as remote agents.

I'm checking whether to load the agent module via ESM import with a type declaration or just use `createRequire` for a CJS-style require, since tsx should handle either depending on package.json's module type. I also realize I need to think through how the staging worker running on the same primary box would interact with this sweep logic, since it shares the physical machine but operates against a different database.

Since the staging DB likely has no reservation records, the sweep there should be a no-op and leave primary nodes alone — but I need to confirm staging-created VMs on the primary don't get missed by the production sweep's node-wide enforcement, since that sweep confines every non-reserved VM on a node regardless of which environment created it.

Platform VMs not tracked in the DB (like hosting-1 or mail on primary) also fall under the node's shared reservation set, while templates stay excluded and stopped VMs only get config changes without live enforcement. For cadence, I'm leaning toward a sweep interval of one to two minutes, since provisioning already applies reservations immediately and the sweep mainly serves as drift detection.

I need to define what counts as drift: a config mismatch, a live thread mismatch, or any non-reserved VM whose live core allocation overlaps with a reservation's CPUs. When drift is found, I'll alert admins (deduplicated by title), log it, and record details like lastDriftAt and lastVerifiedAt on the CpuReservation record. I also need to handle the case where the sweep can't reach an agent at all, like an outdated version returning a 404, by raising an alert that reservations can't be enforced on that node.

For provisioning safety, I want fail-closed behavior: if a node has reservations and applying them fails, I should throw before the VM starts so it never runs unprotected. For nodes without reservations, the desired affinity is null, but I need to watch for cases where a restored VM's archived config still carries an old affinity setting — I should clear that since it could pin the VM awkwardly even if it's not a security problem. Clearing affinity on restore might require root-level API access though, so if that's unavailable I'll just log a warning and let the restore proceed, while double-checking whether Proxmox's `/qemu` restore endpoint actually enforces root privileges when the archived config includes an `affinity` field.

I also need to account for restoring syntech's VPS backups — if the archive's `qemu-server.conf` includes affinity and the token lacks root, the restore could fail outright, so that's a risk worth flagging for staging tests. The same logic needs to apply after resizing cores on a reserved VM, and after snapshot rollbacks: if the snapshot predates the reservation, the old affinity comes back, so I'll re-apply the ensure step before the VM starts again, keeping in mind rollback leaves the VM stopped unless it's a vmstate snapshot. The vm-move action should route through the same start wrapper, and next I'm thinking through how unsuspend and start power actions tie into this flow.

I'm leaning toward skipping the ensure step on plain START for existing VMs since config drift gets corrected by the sweep within a minute anyway, and forcing an agent call on every reserved-node start risks blocking customer starts if the agent is down — better to keep the fix scoped to creation/recreation paths as the tests expect. For the scheduler, I'm adding an optional vcpu parameter to the detailed node scheduling function so reserved-node placement can account for CPU count, which means updating the call sites in region placement, custom-plan, and nxcloud to pass vcpu through consistently.

content.thinking:
I'm planning out the code structure, starting with a pure utility module for parsing and validating CPU set strings with strict formatting rules like ascending ranges and a max CPU limit.

I also need to model the physical topology, grouping threads into socket/core pairs, then build validation logic that checks reservations don't overlap, cover whole cores, and leave at least one shared core free, along with warnings for vCPU mismatches.

From there I'm working out helper functions: one to compute the shared (unreserved) CPU complement, one to determine a VM's desired affinity based on whether it's reserved or in the shared pool, one to diff desired versus actual thread assignments, and one to detect cases where a non-owner VM is improperly sharing reserved CPUs.

Now I'm figuring out scheduler-side math: computing pool/reserved/shared thread counts, headroom percentages for placement decisions, and candidate ranking logic, with the pure scheduling pieces split into their own module for testability. I'm also sketching schema additions — a CpuReservation model, new Node fields for topology snapshots, a CPU_AFFINITY job type, and the relations tying reservations to servers and nodes — while noting that mapping reservation to vmid needs care since the target vmid can change during a migration.

I'm working through what happens to a reservation after a server moves nodes: if the reservation's nodeId no longer matches the server's current nodeId, I'm treating it as stale/inactive, surfacing a UI warning to release or recreate it, and letting the old node's shared pool reclaim those now-idle cores. But I'm second-guessing this — if the move gets rolled back, the reservation should reactivate and re-confine the pool, so I'm considering a safer alternative where reservations stay "held" regardless of the server's current node.

I settle on keeping reservations held for their original node no matter what, with the UI simply flagging that the server has moved — it's simpler and more predictable, even if some cores sit idle.

Now I'm sketching the v5 agent endpoints for CPU topology, affinity queries, and setting VM affinity, plus the node-agent client wrappers and the start of a cpu-affinity worker module that resolves the primary CPU host via the local node-agent.

Writing worker logic for computing desired affinity, enforcing it before VM start, sweeping nodes with reservations to detect and fix drift, and processing affinity jobs (apply, release, refresh-topology, sync-node) that re-validate against live topology and confine non-reserved VMs...

I also need topology refreshed for unreserved nodes so the UI can show available cores — triggered either by an admin action or a periodic sweep. I'll have the sweep refresh topology for every enabled node older than 6 hours, best-effort, silently skipping and recording failures from older agents that return 404.

Next I'm planning the scheduler updates in lib/node-capacity.ts, then the admin UI: a "CPU reservation" card on the Server Compute tab with a client component showing core chips, live validation, and server actions to set/release reservations; and a node-page card showing per-core reservation status, shared pool usage ratio, and buttons to re-sync topology, backed by server actions in a new actions-cpu-reservation.ts file.

Then I'm listing tests to add — pure logic tests, placement tests, agent affinity tests covering exported validation, invalid HTTP inputs, and fake-system apply, plus a source-path test — followed by docs.

For the agent's behavior, I'm working through how `qm set --affinity` applies to running VMs (with live taskset applied regardless), how deletion of affinity reverts to all online CPUs, and the validation rules the agent needs: vmid range checks, requiring a local config file, refusing templates, and enforcing a canonical cpuset format.

I'm also deciding the agent should only validate format and online-CPU membership, leaving cross-reservation business rules to the worker. For applying affinity I'm verifying the PID via /proc/pid/cmdline matching the exact vmid token, then using `taskset -a -p -c` to set affinity across all threads at once since new threads inherit it, and confirming via each thread's Cpus_allowed_list. I'm also noting the exported functions the agent will expose, like reading CPU topology and VM affinities.

One concern: requiring index.js at the top level in the worker will execute module-level code, so I need to make sure the token check and server startup are guarded by a `require.main === module` check, and that any TLS setup happens lazily rather than at import time.

For the topology representation, the agent returns per-thread CPU info with siblings lists, and since core_id is only unique within a socket, I should group physical cores by their sibling set rather than by socket:core key — that's more robust. Then I'm thinking through default settings like scheduling mode and overcommit ratio.

For scheduler inputs, I need per-node thread counts pulled from topology stored in the DB, falling back to a neutral CPU score if topology data is missing for a node rather than doing an expensive live fetch across all nodes.

The topology sweep itself refreshes on every node once agent v5 is deployed, but nodes without the agent still lack this data. As a fallback, I can have the sweep query the Proxmox API's node status endpoint for cpuinfo when the agent isn't available, storing that as a lighter-weight topology source.

For scoring, committed vCPU on a shared pool would sum active servers' vcpu excluding those with explicit reservations, and I'd score candidates by projected RAM and CPU percentages — using a minimax approach that picks whichever node's busiest dimension after placement stays lowest, breaking ties by free RAM.

For hard guards, I need to exclude nodes where planned vCPU plus existing committed vCPU exceeds shared threads times the overcommit ratio, and also consider adding a per-VM rule preventing a single VM from requesting more vCPU than some multiple of the shared thread count, since otherwise each vCPU could end up starved for thread time.

Actually, too many knobs — I'll skip that extra rule and rely on the ratio cap alone, noting node-6's 8-vCPU total capacity for documentation purposes.

In score mode I'm keeping CPU excluded from "roomy" calculations on non-reserved nodes to avoid flipping sold-out status unexpectedly for customers, and I want to document that decision clearly. For regionAvailability, I'm considering adding an optional vcpu parameter (defaulting conservatively to 1) so existing callers that only pass RAM still work while reserved-node guards can still apply.

Looking at node-6's actual numbers — 56084 MB capacity, 32768 MB committed to syntech, 23316 MB free — I'm tracing through what happens in sgp1: with primary and node-3 not accepting provisions, and node-4 over capacity on RAM, node-6 ends up being the only roomy node, so all sgp1 orders funnel there. Once a CPU guard kicks in and a handful of new VMs consume node-6's 8 vCPU, it gets excluded too, and I need to figure out whether that correctly falls back to node-4 or incorrectly reports sold_out under strict mode, comparing that against the current pre-change behavior where RAM alone determines availability.

I decide excluded-by-CPU-guard nodes should be hard-removed from candidates, same as the RAM guard, since overloading the reserved node's shared pool threads hurts the host itself — node-4 remains available as a non-roomy fallback. With "off" mode this should behave identically to the legacy logic. Now I'm ready to start writing the CPU reservation module.

content.thinking:
With allowJs enabled but only typescript files included, the plain JS file won't be typechecked unless it's actually imported, so I'll just import it directly with a default import since esModuleInterop handles the CJS module.exports interop cleanly.

Now I'm sketching out the worker module: defining types for CPU nodes and hosts, a function to fetch reservations for a given node from the database, and the core `ensureVmAffinityBeforeStart` function that checks sandbox mode, falls back to unmanaged behavior when there's no node record, and otherwise reads the node's CPU topology and existing reservations to decide how to handle affinity when starting a VM.

I'm working through the fail-closed logic — if there's no existing reservation, best-effort read current affinity state and clear it if configured; if a reservation exists, compute the desired affinity, apply it to the host, then verify the host actually reports that configuration (and matching live thread assignment if running), throwing a clear error if anything doesn't match. I'm also noting that this assumes the worker runs as root on whichever node it's targeting, which holds for both primary and staging environments, and that nodes aren't clustered so there's no cross-node conf ambiguity.

Now I'm designing the `cpuAffinitySweep()` function, starting with topology refresh logic: for each enabled node whose topology is stale or missing, try querying the agent directly, falling back to the Proxmox API's node status endpoint for CPU count when the agent is too old, only doing so if there's no existing topology already recorded.

For nodes with active reservations, I'm sequencing through: listing current VMs, computing desired affinity per VM, detecting drift, applying fixes, and checking for sharing violations both before and after the fix so nothing slips through. I'm also planning the reservation record updates (lastVerifiedAt vs lastDriftAt) and the admin alert conditions — sharing violations, unreachable nodes, or nodes too outdated to enforce reservations — plus deciding that template-flagged VMs are the only exclusion from affinity management rather than a hardcoded vmid range. Finally I'm sketching the job handler `cpuAffinityJob()` with its operation types (apply, release, sync-node, refresh-topology) and starting to define what refresh-topology does.

For apply and sync-node, I'm having the job call the same node sync logic used by the sweep, storing the result on the payload; for apply specifically, I want the job to re-validate the reservation against the live topology rather than trusting the cached one, but on failure I've decided the job should just fail with an error and leave the reservation row intact so the sweep can still try to enforce it later rather than deleting it — topology changes are unlikely anyway. For release, since the reservation row is already deleted by the action itself, the job's only responsibility is to re-sync the node, clearing affinity settings on non-template VMs if no reservations remain.

I'm sketching what syncNode should return — a summary object with the VMs touched, which ones got fixed, sharing state before/after, and any errors — and reasoning that job failures should simply throw so the existing retry mechanism (up to 3 attempts) handles them, with actions writing their own audit records and jobs writing a separate audit log row with the result.

Now I'm turning to provisioning hooks and the other operations that need affinity handling — vm-move, restore, snapshot rollback, resize — and working out how vm-move's node lookup fits together, since MoveNode has a different shape than AgentNode (it includes isPrimary alongside the usual connection fields). I'm deciding ensureVmAffinityBeforeStart should accept a node-like object and simply reload the fresh node row from the database by id to get accurate topology and connection info rather than relying on whatever was passed in.

I'm settling on a signature like ensureVmAffinityBeforeStart({ nodeId, vmid, why }) that loads the node row itself, and handling the edge case where there's no Node row (primary host without one) by treating it as unmanaged. Time to actually write this out.

import type { Prisma } from "@prisma/client";
import { db } from "./db";

/**
 * Serialise "is a job already in flight for this server? if not, enqueue one"
 * per server, across every web process.
 *
 * WHY THIS EXISTS (found 2026-09-30, reproduced on staging): the "one in-flight
 * job per server" guard in `serverAction` (lib/actions.ts) and `gamePower`
 * (lib/actions-game-control.ts) was a plain `count()` followed by a separate
 * `create()`. Two requests landing within the same few milliseconds both saw
 * zero in-flight jobs and both enqueued — 10 simultaneous Reboot requests
 * against one staging VPS produced 3 REBOOT jobs, and 10 simultaneous game
 * Restarts produced 2 GAME_POWER jobs. A single browser tab can't hit this
 * (Next.js dispatches one Server Action at a time per client), but two tabs, a
 * double-submitting script or a flaky retrying proxy can — and a duplicate
 * START on an already-running VM fails in Proxmox, which after three attempts
 * flips the server to ERROR even though nothing is actually wrong.
 *
 * Wrapping the check + enqueue in a transaction that first takes a
 * transaction-scoped Postgres advisory lock keyed on the server id makes the
 * second request wait until the first has committed its job, so its own count
 * then sees it and it is refused like any other overlapping click. The lock
 * releases automatically on commit/rollback.
 *
 * Key: the two-int form `(namespace, hashtext(serverId))`. Postgres keeps the
 * two-int and single-bigint advisory key spaces separate, so this can never
 * collide with lib/ipam.ts's single-key allocator lock; a hashtext collision
 * between two server ids only means those two servers briefly serialise, never
 * a wrong answer. `pg_advisory_xact_lock` returns `void`, which Prisma's
 * $queryRaw can't deserialize — hence the subselect (same workaround ipam.ts
 * documents).
 */
const SERVER_JOB_LOCK_NAMESPACE = 7301;
const LOCK_SQL = `SELECT 1 AS locked FROM (SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(${SERVER_JOB_LOCK_NAMESPACE}, hashtext($1))) _lock`;

The sequence continues with pushing an additive schema change, deploying through staging then promoting, letting the sweep refresh topology so node-6 picks up its thread map, verifying the topology data, and only then inserting the backfill row. After that, the sweep should confirm VM 667 already matches with no changes needed, checking the worker log for zero fixes and an updated lastVerifiedAt timestamp. Finally, I'll disable the old reservation timer, confirm a test provision lands correctly, and clean up the old files. I'm drafting the SQL insert for the backfill row itself and need to be careful about proper value interpolation.

I also need to check that the interim timer and the sweep running simultaneously won't conflict, since they both converge on the same shared values of 3,7 for this server — so there's no fighting between them. The cpuunits setting of 10000 stays outside this system's management and belongs in config, worth noting separately.

Order matters here: topology must be confirmed before the backfill row is inserted, because if the row goes in while topology is still null, desiredAffinity calculations for other reservations would fail due to no shared pool, causing provisions on node-6 to fail closed and the sweep to throw errors. On first deploy, since topology is null, it gets read immediately rather than waiting for the normal six-hour refresh interval. For nodes lacking an agent token, or running an older agent version that 404s, the system falls back to pve status calls — and if that fallback also fails, it just retries cheaply every minute.

Now I'm working out node-6's actual capacity: the shared pool gives it 2 threads which also serve host, with a ratio pointing to an 8 vCPU budget, and roughly 23.3GB of RAM headroom before hitting the 90% critical threshold, leaving about 17.7GB more before it's no longer "roomy." Realistically this fits a handful of light VPS or small game servers, but CPU-heavy titles like modded Minecraft, ARK, or Rust should be avoided there since they'd contend hard on just 2 threads. I'm also noticing that node-6 is currently the only roomy node in sgp1 — node-4 is over RAM at 132% and both primary and node-3 aren't accepting — so all sgp1 orders funnel to node-6 until its 8 vCPU budget is exhausted, after which they'd spill to node-4 under non-strict least-bad logic, even though strict regionAvailability would already report sgp1 as sold_out once node-6's roomy count hits zero — and this sold-out condition already applies today based on RAM alone.

cat >> /tank/nxeon-wt-cpures/docs/DOCUMENTATION.md <<'EOF'

## Exclusive CPU reservations + CPU-aware placement (2026-10-06, branch `feature/cpu-reservations`, NOT deployed)

**Why.** syntech-vps (VM 667, node-6, i7-7700K 4C/8T, SMT pairs (0,4) (1,5) (2,6) (3,7)) was promised in writing 3 dedicated physical cores (threads `0-2,4-6`), with no other customer's VM ever scheduled on them, kept on renewal, while node-6 keeps taking other customers. Until this ships that promise is held by an interim root timer on node-6 (`/etc/nxeon/cpu-reserve.conf`, `/usr/local/sbin/nxeon-cpu-reserve.sh`, `nxeon-cpu-reserve.timer`, every 30 s), which leaves a gap of up to 30 s in which a newly started VM runs on every thread. The platform's Proxmox token cannot set `affinity` (PVE returns 500; root@pam only).

**Model (additive).** `CpuReservation` (one row per reserved server: `serverId` unique, `nodeId`, canonical `cpuset`, `note`, `createdById`, `lastVerifiedAt`, `lastDriftAt`, `lastDriftDetail`) is the single source of truth. `Node.cpuTopology` (Json: every thread with core/socket/SMT siblings, `source` agent|local|pve) + `Node.cpuTopologyAt`. The shared pool is never stored; it is always topology minus the node's reservations. New `JobType.CPU_AFFINITY` (`payload.op`: apply | release | sync-node | refresh-topology). A reservation stays bound to its node: if the server is moved it keeps holding those cores (both admin pages flag it) until released.

**Rules** (`lib/cpu-reservation.ts validateReservation`, re-run by the server action AND by the worker against the live topology): valid cpuset; topology with a sibling map (agent v5 or the primary); every cpu exists; whole physical cores only (both SMT siblings); no overlap with another reservation; at least one whole core stays shared (never the last core). vCPU ≠ reserved thread count is a warning.

**Desired affinity** (`desiredAffinity`): a node with no reservations is unmanaged (affinity left unset). On a node with reservations every non-template VM is managed: the owner gets its set, every other VM gets the shared pool. No pool computable → throw (fail closed).

**Applying it — no gap.** `ensureVmAffinityBeforeStart` (worker/cpu-affinity.ts) runs right before the Proxmox start in every path that creates or recreates a VM config: `provision` (and so REINSTALL), `resize` (cold cycle), snapshot rollback (restores the snapshot's config), `worker/restore.ts` (qmrestore replaces the config), and the VM-move hypervisor `start` adapter (target start and rollback start; `affinity` is not a carried config key). On a node with reservations it sets config + live threads and re-reads; any failure throws, so the VM is not started. On a node without reservations it only clears a leftover affinity (e.g. restored from a reserved VM's archive), best-effort. `test/cpu-affinity-paths.test.ts` fails if a start in those paths is not preceded by the step.

**Who sets it.** Node agent v5 (node-agent/index.js), three narrowly scoped endpoints: `GET /v1/cpu/topology` (read /sys), `GET /v1/cpu/affinity[?vmid]` (each local VM's effective config affinity incl. `[PENDING]`, plus every live QEMU thread's `Cpus_allowed_list` from /proc), `POST /v1/vm/affinity {vmid, cpuset|null}` → `qm set <vmid> --affinity <set>` (or `--delete affinity`) and, if running, `taskset -a -p -c <set> <pid>`. Strict validation: integer vmid 100..999999999 with a config on THIS node, never a template; cpuset digits/commas/ascending ranges only, every cpu online; argv only (no shell); the pid must carry `-id <vmid>` in its cmdline before taskset touches it. It cannot start/stop/change anything else. The primary (no agent) runs the SAME code: the worker `require`s node-agent/index.js (which now only starts its HTTPS server when run directly) and executes it locally as root.

**Enforcement + drift.** Sweep `cpu-affinity` (every minute): for each node with a reservation, list every VM, fix any config or live-thread drift, record `lastVerifiedAt` / `lastDriftAt` + detail on the reservation, and notify admins: "CPU reservation drift fixed on <node>" when another VM could reach a reserved core and was fixed, "CPU reservation BREACHED" when it could not be fixed, "CPU reservations NOT being enforced on <node>" when the node cannot be read (agent < v5, unreachable). Also refreshes `Node.cpuTopology` on every enabled node every 6 h (agent/local; falls back to a thread count from the Proxmox API for agents < v5). When a node's last reservation is released, the release job clears affinity on every non-template VM on that node.

**CPU-aware placement** (`lib/cpu-placement.ts`, used by `scheduleNodeDetailed`). Setting `cpu_sched_mode`: `score` (default) | `guard` | `off` (exact legacy RAM-only, the rollback switch); `cpu_overcommit_ratio` (default 4 vCPU per thread). In guard/score a node WITH reservations is dropped unless the VM's vCPU fit its shared pool's budget (shared threads × ratio; vCPU of reservation owners excluded), and counts as "roomy" only under the critical threshold on that pool too. In score, candidates are ranked by the lower of their worst projected dimension (max of RAM %, CPU %), ties by free RAM. CPU only ranks nodes without reservations; it never makes them full, so plain vCPU overcommit (node-4 runs ~5 vCPU/thread) never flips a region to sold out. Region-bound strict behaviour and the live RAM guard are unchanged. `vcpu` is passed by VPS orders, game orders (game plan cores), custom plans and NxCloud; `regionAvailability` takes an optional `vcpu`.

**What node-6 can take for other customers.** Shared pool = core 3 (threads 3,7) — shared with the host itself (ZFS, pveproxy, the agent). At ratio 4: 8 vCPU of other VMs in total; RAM ≈ 23 GB uncommitted (56 084 MB capacity − 32 768 MB syntech). Realistic: a handful of light 1–2 vCPU VPS / small game servers. Not CPU-heavy games (modded Minecraft, ARK, Rust): 2 threads would be contended. Today node-6 is the only roomy node in sgp1 (node-4 is over-committed on RAM, primary and node-3 do not accept provisions), so sgp1 orders land there until its 8 vCPU are used; then the region falls back to node-4 (non-strict) and `regionAvailability` will report sgp1 as sold out, the same as when RAM fills.

**Admin UI.** Server → Compute tab → "CPU reservation": pick physical cores from the node's real topology (cores held by another reservation are disabled), live validation, note, Reserve/Update/Release (audited `cpu_reservation.set|release`, then a CPU_AFFINITY job; the job writes `cpu_reservation.job_<op>` with its result). VM config summary now shows `affinity` and `cpuunits`. Node page → "CPU reservations": core map (owner or shared pool), reserved set, shared pool, vCPU committed to the shared pool vs budget, verification state, "Read topology" / "Re-sync affinities now". Settings → Provisioning: the two scheduler settings.

**Rollout (in this order).**
1. `npm run db:push` (additive: table `CpuReservation`, `Node.cpuTopology`, `Node.cpuTopologyAt`, enum value `CPU_AFFINITY`).
2. Upgrade the agent to v5 on every non-primary node BEFORE any reservation row exists: `scp node-agent/index.js root@<node>:/opt/nxeon-agent/index.js && ssh root@<node> systemctl restart nxeon-node-agent`, then `GET /v1/health` must say `version: 5` (`scripts/verify-node.sh` flags code drift). Restarting the agent does not touch VMs. Do node-6 first, then the rest one at a time. Without a reservation on a node, an old agent only means "no leftover-affinity check" (logged, never blocks).
3. Deploy through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → `scripts/promote-production.sh`.
4. Within a minute the sweep writes `Node.cpuTopology`; confirm node-6's has 8 threads with siblings before step 5 (a reservation on a node without a sibling map makes every new VM there fail closed).
5. Backfill syntech-vps (exact SQL in the 2026-10-06 report / below).
6. Watch `journalctl -u nxeon-worker | grep cpu-affinity` for one sweep: no fixes expected (VM 667 already `0-2,4-6`, nothing else on node-6 yet), and `CpuReservation.lastVerifiedAt` gets set.

```sql
INSERT INTO "CpuReservation" ("id","serverId","nodeId","cpuset","note","createdAt","updatedAt")
VALUES ('cpures-syntech-vps-667','1d53b89c-b4e7-4a3a-bd3a-2f75f4050003','cmuw1x5o50000hlr0xtmx60xs','0-2,4-6',
        'syntech-vps: 3 dedicated physical cores (0-2,4-6), promised in writing, kept on renewal; adopted from the interim node-6 cpu-reserve timer 2026-10-06',
        now(), now());
```

**Retiring the interim node-6 timer** (after step 6, and after a throwaway VM provisioned on node-6 is seen confined to `3,7` before its first start): `systemctl disable --now nxeon-cpu-reserve.timer`, then `rm /etc/systemd/system/nxeon-cpu-reserve.{timer,service} /usr/local/sbin/nxeon-cpu-reserve.sh /etc/nxeon/cpu-reserve.conf && systemctl daemon-reload`. The two can run side by side without fighting (both compute shared = `3,7`), so there is no rush.

**Not handled / known limits.** Host processes (ZFS, pveproxy, the agent) still run on all threads, reserved ones included; this guarantees no other VM, not an idle core. `cpuunits` (10000 on VM 667) is not managed here; it is a plain config value the token can set and a move does not carry it. A restore of an archive that contains `affinity` goes through the API token; whether PVE refuses that for a non-root token is unverified, so test a restore of a throwaway reserved VM on staging before relying on it. VMs created outside the platform (manual `qm create` + start) are confined by the next sweep (≤ 1 min), not before start.

**Files:** `prisma/schema.prisma`, `lib/cpu-reservation.ts`, `lib/cpu-placement.ts`, `lib/node-capacity.ts`, `lib/region-placement.ts`, `lib/order.ts`, `lib/game-order.ts`, `lib/custom-plan.ts`, `lib/actions-nxcloud.ts`, `lib/settings.ts`, `lib/actions-settings.ts`, `lib/node-agent.ts`, `lib/actions-cpu-reservation.ts`, `node-agent/index.js`, `worker/cpu-affinity.ts`, `worker/index.ts`, `worker/restore.ts`, `worker/vm-move.ts`, `components/admin/CpuReservationControls.tsx`, `components/admin/server360/tabs/ComputeTab.tsx`, `components/admin/settings/ProvisioningPanel.tsx`, `app/admin/nodes/[id]/page.tsx`. Tests: `test/cpu-reservation.test.ts`, `test/cpu-placement.test.ts`, `test/node-agent-cpu-affinity.test.ts` (fake /sys, /proc, conf dir and recording exec; the real agent process only gets refused or read-only requests), `test/cpu-affinity-paths.test.ts`.
EOF

**Who sets it.** Node agent v5 (node-agent/index.js), three narrowly scoped endpoints: `GET /v1/cpu/topology` (read /sys), `GET /v1/cpu/affinity[?vmid]` (each local VM's effective config affinity incl. `[PENDING]`, plus every live QEMU thread's `Cpus_allowed_list` from /proc), `POST /v1/vm/affinity {vmid, cpuset|null}` → `qm set <vmid> --affinity <set>` (or `--delete affinity`) and, if running, `taskset -a -p -c <set> <pid>`. Strict validation: integer vmid 100..999999999 with a config on THIS node, never a template; cpuset digits/commas/ascending ranges only, every cpu online; argv only (no shell); the pid must carry `-id <vmid>` in its cmdline before taskset touches it. It cannot start/stop/change anything else. The primary (no agent) runs the SAME code: the worker `require`s node-agent/index.js (which now only starts its HTTPS server when run directly) and executes it locally as root.

**Enforcement + drift.** Sweep `cpu-affinity` (every minute): for each node with a reservation, list every VM, fix any config or live-thread drift, record `lastVerifiedAt` / `lastDriftAt` + detail on the reservation, and notify admins: "CPU reservation drift fixed on <node>" when another VM could reach a reserved core and was fixed, "CPU reservation BREACHED" when it could not be fixed, "CPU reservations NOT being enforced on <node>" when the node cannot be read (agent < v5, unreachable). Also refreshes `Node.cpuTopology` on every enabled node every 6 h (agent/local; falls back to a thread count from the Proxmox API for agents < v5). When a node's last reservation is released, the release job clears affinity on every non-template VM on that node.

**CPU-aware placement** (`lib/cpu-placement.ts`, used by `scheduleNodeDetailed`). Setting `cpu_sched_mode`: `score` (default) | `guard` | `off` (exact legacy RAM-only, the rollback switch); `cpu_overcommit_ratio` (default 4 vCPU per thread). In guard/score a node WITH reservations is dropped unless the VM's vCPU fit its shared pool's budget (shared threads × ratio; vCPU of reservation owners excluded), and counts as "roomy" only under the critical threshold on that pool too. In score, candidates are ranked by the lower of their worst projected dimension (max of RAM %, CPU %), ties by free RAM. CPU only ranks nodes without reservations; it never makes them full, so plain vCPU overcommit (node-4 runs ~5 vCPU/thread) never flips a region to sold out. Region-bound strict behaviour and the live RAM guard are unchanged. `vcpu` is passed by VPS orders, game orders (game plan cores), custom plans and NxCloud; `regionAvailability` takes an optional `vcpu`.

**What node-6 can take for other customers.** Shared pool = core 3 (threads 3,7) — shared with the host itself (ZFS, pveproxy, the agent). At ratio 4: 8 vCPU of other VMs in total; RAM ≈ 23 GB uncommitted (56 084 MB capacity − 32 768 MB syntech). Realistic: a handful of light 1–2 vCPU VPS / small game servers. Not CPU-heavy games (modded Minecraft, ARK, Rust): 2 threads would be contended. Today node-6 is the only roomy node in sgp1 (node-4 is over-committed on RAM, primary and node-3 do not accept provisions), so sgp1 orders land there until its 8 vCPU are used; then the region falls back to node-4 (non-strict) and `regionAvailability` will report sgp1 as sold out, the same as when RAM fills.

**Admin UI.** Server → Compute tab → "CPU reservation": pick physical cores from the node's real topology (cores held by another reservation are disabled), live validation, note, Reserve/Update/Release (audited `cpu_reservation.set|release`, then a CPU_AFFINITY job; the job writes `cpu_reservation.job_<op>` with its result). VM config summary now shows `affinity` and `cpuunits`. Node page → "CPU reservations": core map (owner or shared pool), reserved set, shared pool, vCPU committed to the shared pool vs budget, verification state, "Read topology" / "Re-sync affinities now". Settings → Provisioning: the two scheduler settings.

**Rollout (in this order).**
1. `npm run db:push` (additive: table `CpuReservation`, `Node.cpuTopology`, `Node.cpuTopologyAt`, enum value `CPU_AFFINITY`).
2. Upgrade the agent to v5 on every non-primary node BEFORE any reservation row exists: `scp node-agent/index.js root@<node>:/opt/nxeon-agent/index.js && ssh root@<node> systemctl restart nxeon-node-agent`, then `GET /v1/health` must say `version: 5` (`scripts/verify-node.sh` flags code drift). Restarting the agent does not touch VMs. Do node-6 first, then the rest one at a time. Without a reservation on a node, an old agent only means "no leftover-affinity check" (logged, never blocks).
3. Deploy through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → `scripts/promote-production.sh`.
4. Within a minute the sweep writes `Node.cpuTopology`; confirm node-6's has 8 threads with siblings before step 5 (a reservation on a node without a sibling map makes every new VM there fail closed).
5. Backfill syntech-vps (exact SQL in the 2026-10-06 report / below).
6. Watch `journalctl -u nxeon-worker | grep cpu-affinity` for one sweep: no fixes expected (VM 667 already `0-2,4-6`, nothing else on node-6 yet), and `CpuReservation.lastVerifiedAt` gets set.

input.message:
## CPU reservations + CPU-aware placement: built, not deployed or merged

**Branch:** `feature/cpu-reservations` in worktree `/tank/nxeon-wt-cpures`. There are 3 commits on top of main `b23bc8e8d5`, and the post-commit hook pushed the branch to origin:
- `b55e8eb00c`: schema plus the pure cpuset and placement logic
- `a3b2c4de0e`: node-agent v5, the worker apply step, sweep and job, the scheduler, the admin UI and the tests
- `8c06825dd8`: docs

Every commit was staged by explicit path and the tree is clean.

**Checks:**
- `npx tsc --noEmit` exits 0.
- Full suite: 47 failures against the 46-name baseline. The one new name is "HARD STOP at the window's end…" in `test/backup-node-runner.test.ts`. It is a timing test in the backup runner, which I didn't touch. It passed 15/15 three times when run on its own, so it is flaky under full-suite load. No failure output mentions my files.
- My 4 new test files pass (32 tests).

**How I kept prod safe:**
- The worktree's `node_modules` is a real directory: symlinks to prod's packages, plus local copies of `.prisma` and `@prisma`. That way `prisma generate` wrote into the worktree only; I confirmed the timestamp on prod's generated client did not change.
- Prod DB was SELECT-only. VM 667 and the interim node-6 timer were never touched; on node-6 I only ran read-only `cat`, `lscpu`, `qm list` and `/proc` reads.

### Design
- **Data model (additive):**
  - New `CpuReservation` table: one row per reserved server (`serverId` unique, `nodeId`, canonical `cpuset`, `note`, `createdById`, `lastVerifiedAt`, `lastDriftAt`/`lastDriftDetail`). This is the single source of truth.
  - `Node.cpuTopology` (Json: each thread with core, socket and SMT siblings, plus its source) and `Node.cpuTopologyAt`.
  - New job type `CPU_AFFINITY`.
  - The shared pool is never stored. It is always computed as topology minus the node's reservations, so the two cannot drift apart.
  - A reservation stays tied to its node: if the server is moved, it keeps holding those cores (both admin pages flag this) until an admin releases it.
- **Rules** (`lib/cpu-reservation.ts`). These run in the admin action and again in the worker against the live topology:
  - only whole physical cores (both SMT siblings);
  - every cpu must exist on the node;
  - no overlap with another reservation;
  - at least one core stays shared, so the last core can never be reserved;
  - the node's topology must include the sibling map (agent v5 or the primary).
  - A vCPU count that doesn't match the reserved thread count is only a warning.
- **Desired affinity:**
  - A node with no reservations is left alone.
  - On a node with reservations, every non-template VM is managed: the owner gets its set, every other VM gets the shared pool.
  - If the shared pool can't be computed, it fails closed (refuses rather than leaving a VM unconfined).
- **No gap at creation.** `ensureVmAffinityBeforeStart` (`worker/cpu-affinity.ts`) runs right before the Proxmox start in every path that creates or replaces a VM's config:
  - provision (which reinstall also uses)
  - resize, before its cold start
  - snapshot rollback
  - backup restore (`worker/restore.ts`)
  - the VM-move start step, for both the target and a rollback; `affinity` is not one of the config keys a move carries over.
  - On a node with reservations it sets config and live threads, reads them back, and throws if they don't match, so the VM is never started unconfined.
  - On other nodes it only clears a leftover affinity, best-effort.
  - `test/cpu-affinity-paths.test.ts` fails if any start in those paths lacks the step.
- **Node agent v5** gets three narrow endpoints:
  - `GET /v1/cpu/topology`: reads /sys.
  - `GET /v1/cpu/affinity[?vmid]`: each VM's config affinity (including `[PENDING]`) plus every live QEMU thread's `Cpus_allowed_list`.
  - `POST /v1/vm/affinity {vmid, cpuset|null}`: runs `qm set --affinity` or `--delete affinity`, plus `taskset -a -p -c` on a running VM.
  - Validation is strict: integer vmid with a config on that node, never a template; cpuset digits, commas and ranges only, every cpu online; commands as argv arrays, no shell; and the pid must carry `-id <vmid>` before `taskset` touches it.
  - It can't do anything else to a VM.
  - The primary runs the same code locally: the worker `require`s `node-agent/index.js`, which now only starts its server when run directly.
- **Drift enforcement:**
  - A `cpu-affinity` sweep runs every minute on each node with a reservation. It checks config and live threads, fixes drift, and records verified/drift times on the row.
  - It sends admin alerts for: drift fixed, "BREACHED" (could not fix), and "NOT being enforced" (agent unreachable or older than v5).
  - It also refreshes topology every 6 hours; for agents older than v5 it falls back to a thread count from the Proxmox API.
- **Placement** (`lib/cpu-placement.ts`, used by `scheduleNodeDetailed`). Setting `cpu_sched_mode`:
  - `score` (default): ranks candidates on both RAM and CPU headroom.
  - `guard`: keeps RAM-only ranking but still enforces the shared-pool limit.
  - `off`: exactly the old RAM-only behaviour (the rollback switch).
  - Setting `cpu_overcommit_ratio`, default 4 vCPU per thread.
  - A node with reservations is dropped unless the VM's vCPU fit its shared pool's budget (shared threads × ratio, not counting the reservation owner).

- `b55e8eb00c`: schema plus the pure cpuset and placement logic
- `a3b2c4de0e`: node-agent v5, the worker apply step, sweep and job, the scheduler, the admin UI and the tests
- `8c06825dd8`: docs

Every commit was staged by explicit path and the tree is clean.

**Checks:**
- `npx tsc --noEmit` exits 0.
- Full suite: 47 failures against the 46-name baseline. The one new name is "HARD STOP at the window's end…" in `test/backup-node-runner.test.ts`. It is a timing test in the backup runner, which I didn't touch. It passed 15/15 three times when run on its own, so it is flaky under full-suite load. No failure output mentions my files.
- My 4 new test files pass (32 tests).

**How I kept prod safe:**
- The worktree's `node_modules` is a real directory: symlinks to prod's packages, plus local copies of `.prisma` and `@prisma`. That way `prisma generate` wrote into the worktree only; I confirmed the timestamp on prod's generated client did not change.
- Prod DB was SELECT-only. VM 667 and the interim node-6 timer were never touched; on node-6 I only ran read-only `cat`, `lscpu`, `qm list` and `/proc` reads.

### Design
- **Data model (additive):**
  - New `CpuReservation` table: one row per reserved server (`serverId` unique, `nodeId`, canonical `cpuset`, `note`, `createdById`, `lastVerifiedAt`, `lastDriftAt`/`lastDriftDetail`). This is the single source of truth.
  - `Node.cpuTopology` (Json: each thread with core, socket and SMT siblings, plus its source) and `Node.cpuTopologyAt`.
  - New job type `CPU_AFFINITY`.
  - The shared pool is never stored. It is always computed as topology minus the node's reservations, so the two cannot drift apart.
  - A reservation stays tied to its node: if the server is moved, it keeps holding those cores (both admin pages flag this) until an admin releases it.
- **Rules** (`lib/cpu-reservation.ts`). These run in the admin action and again in the worker against the live topology:
  - only whole physical cores (both SMT siblings);
  - every cpu must exist on the node;
  - no overlap with another reservation;
  - at least one core stays shared, so the last core can never be reserved;
  - the node's topology must include the sibling map (agent v5 or the primary).

- **Desired affinity:**
